destination.title: The Fine Print That Quietly Took Your Right to Sue

short12: You probably gave up your right to sue, the moment you tapped "I agree."
Buried in your phone, bank, and job contracts is one clause: disputes go to private arbitration.
It started with about thirty dollars in tax on a "free" phone.
Small harms only matter when people can join together.
In 2011, the Supreme Court said companies can enforce this.
In 2018, it reached the workplace too.
Two ordinary rights, gone, in a line nobody reads.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: They sign up with AT&T for cellphones advertised as "free." Then the bill comes, and they have been charged about thirty dollars in sales tax on those "free" phones .
You tap "I agree." You do not read it — almost no one does .
In 2011, a fight over about thirty dollars turned that clause into the law of the land .
And it usually adds a second piece: a class-action waiver, a promise that you will never band together with other people who were harmed the same way .
To understand the case, you have to understand two things: a 1925 law, and one small, powerful sentence.
The 1925 law is the Federal Arbitration Act.
And for the small, scattered harms we just described, "one person at a time" can mean, in practice, "no one at all," because no individual claim is large enough to pursue .
In 2011, the Supreme Court sided with AT&T.

Lewis, in 2018, by another five-to-four vote, with Justice Neil Gorsuch writing, the Court held that employers, too, can require employees to arbitrate individually and waive class or collective actions — and that doing so does not violate federal labor law .
Two ordinary rights — to sue in open court, and to join with others — are now, for most people, waivable by a sentence almost no one reads.

shorts.angle: Both rulings were five to four, and the dissents said what the majorities would not: for a claim worth a few dollars, taking away the class action does not change the forum, it ends the case.
shorts.type: C — the dissents, one of them read aloud from the bench
shorts.avoids: The existing Short lists the clause, the thirty dollars and both decisions. It never says either ruling was contested, what the dissenting justices argued the waiver actually does, or that one dissent was read from the bench.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The 1925 law that made all of this possible, and why it sat quiet for most of a century before companies found it.
shorts.loop_join: L5 ends on the count that did not change, and L1 gives that count on the restart: four justices lost twice, one read hers aloud.

lines.text: Four justices lost this fight twice. One read her dissent out loud from the bench.
source_lines: she read part of it aloud from the bench, a step justices reserve for the rulings they most strongly oppose

lines.text: In 2011 the Court sided with AT&T, five to four. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote it. A state cannot refuse to enforce a class action waiver because it finds it unfair.
source_lines: In 2011, the Supreme Court sided with AT&T. By a vote of five to four, it held that the Federal Arbitration Act preempts California's rule — that a state cannot refuse to enforce a class-action waiver just because it finds the waiver unfair.
The opinion was written by Justice Antonin Scalia.

lines.text: Justice Stephen Breyer dissented. For claims worth a few dollars, the class action is often the only realistic way to hold a large company accountable. Take that away, and the case may end before it starts.
source_lines: For claims worth only a few dollars each, he argued, the class action is often the only realistic way to hold a large company accountable at all. Take it away, and you have not just changed the forum — you may have ended the case before it starts.

lines.text: Seven years later the Court extended it to your job. Ruth Bader Ginsburg read part of her dissent aloud from the bench, a step justices reserve for the rulings they most strongly oppose.
source_lines: In Epic Systems v. Lewis, in 2018, by another five-to-four vote, with Justice Neil Gorsuch writing, the Court held that employers, too, can require employees to arbitrate individually and waive class or collective actions
Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote a forceful dissent
she read part of it aloud from the bench, a step justices reserve for the rulings they most strongly oppose

lines.text: She argued that facing an employer one at a time ignores why federal law lets workers act together.
source_lines: Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote a forceful dissent, arguing that forcing employees to face their employer one at a time ignored the very reason federal law lets workers act together

lines.text: The waiver forces every claim to be brought one person at a time, which for small scattered harms can mean no one at all.
source_lines: The waiver does something more: it forces every claim to be brought one person at a time.
because no individual claim is large enough to pursue

lines.text: Those clauses are now standard in contracts for a phone, a bank account, and very often a job.
source_lines: Mandatory arbitration clauses, with class-action waivers, are now a standard feature of American life

lines.text: Both rulings stand. The dissents are just dissents, and reading one aloud does not change the count.

shorts.angle: You never signed the clause at all: it attaches when you activate a phone, open an account or show up for your first day of work, and there is a serious argument that this is fine.
shorts.type: A — second-person threat, with the other side stated honestly
shorts.avoids: The existing Short frames it as tapping 'I agree' and lists the two rulings. It never explains that the clause attaches through ordinary acts like starting a job, that the terms are take it or leave it, or that defenders have a real case.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Where lawmakers and regulators are still fighting to claw this back, and for which kinds of claims.
shorts.loop_join: L5 asks for the moment of agreement, and L1 answers that there was none, only a first day of work.

lines.text: You never signed it. You showed up for your first day of work.
source_lines: You do not sign these clauses with a pen at a desk. You accept them by activating a phone, opening an account, clicking a box, or showing up for your first day of work.

lines.text: You do not sign these clauses with a pen at a desk. You accept them by activating a phone, opening an account, or starting a job.
source_lines: You do not sign these clauses with a pen at a desk. You accept them by activating a phone, opening an account, clicking a box, or showing up for your first day of work.

lines.text: The law treats that as a real agreement, and the terms are not negotiable. Take it or leave it, and leaving it can mean going without the service, or the job.
source_lines: The law treats that as a real agreement — and for the most part, the terms are not up for negotiation. It is take it or leave it, and "leaving it" can mean going without the service, or the job

lines.text: There is a real argument on the other side. Defenders say arbitration is faster, cheaper, and less formal than a lawsuit, and that claimants sometimes do as well or better.
source_lines: Defenders argue the opposite: that arbitration is generally faster, cheaper, and less formal than a lawsuit, that the 1925 law reflects a long-standing policy of honoring agreements people make, and that individual claimants can sometimes do as well or better than they would in a crowded court

lines.text: Critics answer that it can quietly close the courthouse door, leaving widespread small harms with no realistic remedy and no public precedent.
source_lines: can quietly close the courthouse door, leaving widespread small harms with no realistic remedy, decided in private proceedings that set no public precedent

lines.text: The claims about cost, speed and outcomes are genuinely disputed. What the case settled was not who is right, but who decides.
source_lines: are genuinely disputed, and we are not going to pretend one side has settled them. The case is about who decides.

lines.text: Nothing was seized and nobody was punished. This power was handed over voluntarily, in the most ordinary act of modern life.
source_lines: No officer took anything. No school punished anyone.
The power here was handed over voluntarily, in the most ordinary act of modern life: tapping a button to make a screen go away.

lines.text: So find the moment you agreed to any of it. That is the part most people cannot answer.
